rationale:
Quota today: 1 long-form, 3 Shorts, 0 carousels. Every piece is about GLP-1 and tirzepatide, and none is a radar 'reject'.

L1 is the next Lane A topic in the growth playbook's order: "Tirzepatide and Birth Control Pills". Hair Loss and Stopping already shipped. It's an evergreen practical question, and the label, CDC contraception guidance and ACOG cover it in depth, so the body doesn't depend on news. No live Lane A video answers it, and few creators cover it from the label. The Oct 16 pregnancy meta-analysis is the intro hook only.

The three Shorts follow the slot formats:
- **08:00 (S1):** a body-worry "Is this normal?" Short on nail changes. It's an emerging topic with fresh dermatology coverage on Nov 4. Our last nail Short was 35 days ago, so this is outside the 30-day window, and the new fact is that about half of the users had nail problems before starting.
- **13:00 (S2):** the week's one allowed gray-market Short, a retatrutide "what's confirmed" piece with a loop ending. This is the lead format with the proven 209–278 view range. The new fact is the Nov 2 seizure by Malaysia's Health Ministry.
- **20:00 (S3):** the funnel Short and a spin-off of L1. It asks a fresh question (why a slower stomach can affect the pill) that L1 answers.

The mix is 2 emerging or rising pieces, 1 evergreen topic refreshed with a timely hook, and 1 that corrects misleading claims. Pillars are spread out: life-on-glp1 twice, get-the-most once, research once. Body systems are reproductive (2 pieces), skin/nails and none. I left these out on purpose:
- **Thanksgiving:** its peak is still 13–22 days away, so it goes to a later 20:00 slot.
- **Alcohol, menopause and prediabetes:** these are observational, and menopause and prediabetes were covered in the last week. None of them fits a 13:00 lead format.
- **REDEFINE 4:** this waits for the ObesityWeek data on Nov 14–17, when it can qualify for the 48-hour L2 slot.
- **Poison-centre calls and surgery:** guardrail risk, and these topics have performed poorly for us.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and oral birth control pills: what the US prescribing information says about reduced oral hormonal contraceptive exposure (slower gastric emptying), why non-oral methods aren't affected in the same way, how vomiting and diarrhoea can affect any pill, and the label's pregnancy section, with ACOG's Oct 23, 2026 practice advisory for pregnancy planning
pieces.angle: Keep the plan as written, with these changes. (a) Chapter 6: drop the 'Front Pharmacol Oct 16' meta-analysis unless its PubMed or journal abstract can be opened and confirmed. If it can't, use the confirmed Sept 2026 meta-analysis of about 2.1M pregnancies, labelled 'observational, after unplanned exposure around conception, not proof of safety'. (b) Quote the label's contraception sentence word for word, including the 4-week periods. Say 'may reduce', never 'stops working'. (c) Cite the ACOG advisory itself and use its exact wording: consider stopping 1–2 months before trying to conceive, don't use it in pregnancy, and use effective contraception if not planning a pregnancy. (d) Chapter 5: 'The semaglutide labels report no clinically relevant change in pill exposure in their study.' No ranking, and no 'so switch' implication.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Birth Control Pills: What to Know
pieces.why: It's the next Lane A topic in the playbook's queue, no live Lane A video answers it, competition is low, and labels and guidelines can verify it fully. | fact-check: This is a strong Lane A topic with a sound evidence base. The US Zepbound and Mounjaro labels both say tirzepatide can reduce oral hormonal contraceptive exposure because it delays gastric emptying. Both advise switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting and for 4 weeks after each dose increase. Writers must copy the label text, not this paraphrase. The 4-week period is a duration, not a dose, so it may be quoted exactly as printed. Never name mg steps. The semaglutide labels (Wegovy/Ozempic) report no clinically relevant change in oral contraceptive exposure. Present that only as label text, side by side, with no ranking. I confirmed the ACOG GLP-1 pregnancy/lactation advisory exists (Healio 23 Oct 2026). It advises counselling on the lack of safety data, considering stopping 1–2 months before trying to conceive, not using the medicine in pregnancy, and discussing effective contraception because weight loss may improve fertility. Quote ACOG's own document, not the news coverage. I could NOT confirm a Frontiers in Pharmacology meta-analysis dated Oct 16, 2026. Searches turned up a Sept 2026 meta-analysis (about 2.1M pregnancies, City St George's/Leicester) and an Oct 15 scoping review (World J Diabetes). Both are observational, and their authors say the results are 'not proof of safety'. For chapter 4, CDC's US SPR (2024) covers vomiting and diarrhoea with combined pills. Credit CDC only for wording found on the CDC page. Don't say tirzepatide 'makes the pill fail'. Say the label says it 'may reduce' its effectiveness for that period. The GI line, the don't-switch line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line are all required. No 'Ozempic babies'.

pieces.topic: Nail changes on GLP-1 medicines (nail lifting/onycholysis, brittleness): EADV 2026 multinational survey, revisited by The Dermatology Digest on Nov 4, 2026
pieces.angle: Calm 'Is this normal?' Short. Answer: in a self-reported survey presented at the EADV dermatology congress in October 2026 (not yet peer-reviewed), 39% of GLP-1 medicine users reported nail lifting vs 9% of similar non-users (575 vs 1,329 people). Say 'linked to, not proof'. New fact: about half of users said they had nail problems before starting. Add one line: 'Why isn't known yet. Researchers are still looking.' Mention weight loss or eating less only as an unconfirmed idea. Credit EADV, not a secondary blog. Our own untagged tips: enough protein unless your clinician limits it, and gentle nail care. No supplements. See a doctor or dermatologist for pain, swelling, pus or nails that keep lifting. Include the GI line, 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: GLP-1 Medicines and Your Nails: Is This Normal?
pieces.why: It's the proven calm 'Is this normal?' format with a fresh Nov 4 hook and low competition, and the new fact is that many users had nail problems before starting. | fact-check: I verified the core facts. EADV Congress 2026 (Vienna, Sept 30–Oct 3) heard a survey of 575 GLP-1 users vs 1,329 non-users with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity in France, the US, Brazil and Mexico. Nail detachment: 39% vs 9%. About half of users reported nail problems before starting. Nail problems stayed more common even when the analysis was limited to people who had lost weight. That partly weakens a 'fast weight loss' explanation, so if the hypothesis is mentioned it must be worded as the researchers' speculation only. It's a congress abstract and not peer-reviewed: label it so. I didn't verify the Dermatology Digest Nov 4 piece. Credit the EADV congress presentation or the EADV press release instead. Coverage reports the drug class, so keep the title class-level ('GLP-1 medicines') unless the source breaks out tirzepatide.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide 'what's confirmed': Phase 3 results are real, but it isn't approved anywhere, and Malaysia's Health Ministry seized RM341,000 of unapproved retatrutide (Nov 2, 2026)
pieces.angle: Open: 'Is retatrutide approved? Not anywhere, as of Nov 5, 2026.' Fact 1: one Phase 3 result, with trial name, population, arm, placebo figure and timeframe. Use the peer-reviewed paper if one can be opened; otherwise label it 'company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed'. Fact 2: 'On Nov 2, 2026, Malaysia's Health Ministry told Parliament that 12 raids, from 2025 to September 2026, seized 697 units of unapproved retatrutide worth about RM341,000 (The Star).' Online 'research' products aren't the trial drug, and nobody knows what's in them. Lilly plans to file with the FDA in Q1 2027, and a plan to file isn't approval. Better route: ask a prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial. Then the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, with a loop back to the opening question.
pieces.why: Retatrutide 'what's confirmed' Shorts are a proven lead format (209–278 views), there are fresh signals from Nov 2–4, and it uses the week's one gray-market slot. | fact-check: The Malaysia framing as briefed is inaccurate. The Star (2 Nov 2026) and The Sun report that the Health Ministry told Parliament on Nov 2 that 12 raids from 2025 to September 2026 seized 697 units of unapproved retatrutide worth RM341,000. It was not a single seizure on Nov 2. Bernama's 'over RM400,000' figure includes Ozempic products, so don't mix the two numbers. Lilly's plan to file in Q1 2027 is confirmed (pharmaphorum, Lilly investor release). The plan requires a Phase 3 result 'copied from the peer-reviewed paper', but I couldn't confirm a peer-reviewed Phase 3 retatrutide publication. TRIUMPH-1 (2,339 adults with obesity or overweight plus a comorbidity, 80 weeks) was announced as topline results on 21 May 2026. If no peer-reviewed paper can be opened, label the result 'company-reported topline, not yet peer-reviewed'. TRIUMPH-1 is a no-diabetes population, and TRIUMPH-2 is the type 2 diabetes trial. Gray-market rules apply: no sellers, no vials, no doses, no access routes.

pieces.topic: Why a slower stomach can affect birth control pills on tirzepatide: delayed gastric emptying and oral contraceptive absorption, per the US label
pieces.angle: 20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question (the mechanism) rather than re-cutting L1. 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer. Answer within 10 s: tirzepatide slows how fast food leaves your stomach, and the label says this can lower how much of an oral hormonal contraceptive reaches your blood. Copy the label wording exactly. Give no dose numbers and no step-by-step instructions, and match L1's verified script exactly. One line: the label points to non-oral or backup methods for a time, so ask your prescriber which fits you. One GI line. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. No Exp F line and no spoken titles. Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' Put L1's URL on description line 1 only once it's verified live. Otherwise link Side Effects and don't count this Short toward Exp D.
